cards.title: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments

depth.text: someone built a **tax benchmark** to see whether AI agents can handle **messy, end-to-end professional assignments**

The benchmark covers eight areas of tax practice and includes **50 environments and 1,789 files**; agents must investigate conflicting records and produce returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or advice. cards.title: Ten days later, Git on macOS still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates

depth.text: Apple's macOS tools still trust **compromised certificates**, putting Git, curl, and other developer connections at **risk**

Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October, but macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, still trusted the certificates and **undid the workaround** users had applied by hand. Attackers can intercept **HTTPS connections** made by Git, curl and python3, including Git credentials. Apple says updates may revert a manual fix, so developers need to check again after each update.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters see Apple's delay and the manual workaround as a serious security failure; another says the threat is overblown because an attacker would need to compromise a lot to intercept traffic.

comments.text: That MacOS hasn't removed from OS-level /etc/ssl seems like a big deal, effecting more than just OS-supplied git. Is /etc/certs not used by most graphical Mac software, I guess? cards.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware threatens most servers on planet Earth

depth.text: a bug in widely used **server boot firmware** can let attackers **run code** before defenses load

The flaw sits in **EDK II’s PXE network-boot code**: an oversized ICMP error can overwrite memory and let an attacker run code **before the operating system starts**. Exploitation needs network access during PXE boot, and it only applies to systems using EDK II and network boot; machines booting only from disk are not affected.

I've always been downright suspicious of the creation of UEFI. It executes code before the operating system but doesn't really provide a hardware abstraction layer like BIOS does. Most operating system don't use BIOS or any other software layer and configure the hardware themselves. Why is it there then? And unlike BIOS which is relatively small UEFI is "full-fat" almost the size of an operating…

> [...] had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January we will hopefully soon see an end to this sort of naive optimism, especially when it's an ai-assisted/ai-found vulnerability.

An interesting part of this is actually in defeating secure-boot or bitlocker. If a device is misconfigured for PXE boot with an otherwise locked down UEFI system, and strong secure boot. This could let you break the boot-chain and then disable secure-boot or extract keys from a TPM. The main question here is how often devices you'd want to try this against have PXE boot enabled. I'm thinking of…

cards.title: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update

cards.title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean

depth.text: someone turned a huge math proof into **checked code** and **found a gap** along the way

The team formalized the **first-generation proof** in Lean, with **every logical step checked** by Lean’s kernel. During that work, they found **counterexamples** to a closure assertion in a published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem, then gave an alternative argument for the simple-group case.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call this a good use of auto-formalization and say AI companies should fill known gaps; others say LLM formalization is less useful than human formalization.
entities: The Classification of Finite Simple Groups

Maybe my understanding of Lean is wrong; I'm thinking of…

The original proof was a collaboration of ~100 mathematicians, if Tao is correct then we should expect to see more such collaborations in the future like we do in e.g. physics.

depth.text: someone **grew cacao trees** in **Northern California** and shares how to try it at home

The guide recommends **soaking fresh seeds** for 1-2 days until a root starts to poke out, then keeping the soil warm and moist. Flowers need **hand-pollinating**, and baby pods dry out after 6-8 weeks.

comments.text: Cacao trees are the most difficult plant I have grown, they are much more finicky than many others, and I almost only grow tropical or subtropical plants (in a temperate climate, in France and now Belgium). I don't know which climate this gentleman lives in, but winter in France has been fatal to several of my trees simply because of the reduced ambient humidity due to needing heating in the…

I recently tried "ChoViva" it's a chocolate substitute made from sunflower seeds. Turns out 80% of the chocolate flavor comes from the processing, including fermentation and roasting and not from the plant. They process the sunflower seeds in a way that achieves a taste and texture very close to chocolate. In a way, I prefer it over chocolate because it has no caffeine and has a slightly…
Can I just add that this commercial website is great. It's informative. It has lots of information. It's very clear to read. And the blog just breathes loving the product.

glossary.HSI: Homeland Security Investigations: one of ICE’s two parts, which carries out investigations.
glossary.COINTELPRO: Counterintelligence Program: the FBI program the article says surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed social movements.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell: a way to connect to another computer and send it commands over a network.
glossary.doxing: Finding and publishing someone’s private details without permission.
glossary.data broker: A company that gathers information about people and sells or shares it.
glossary.encrypted chat: A conversation scrambled so people without permission can’t read it.
glossary.frontier model: One of the most capable, newest AI models available.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.agentic workflow: A task where an AI takes several steps and acts toward a goal, rather than just replying once.
glossary.prompt injection: Instructions hidden in text or a file that try to trick an AI into ignoring its intended directions.
glossary.long-horizon: A task that takes many steps or a long time to finish.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.humanist: Someone who follows humanism, an outlook that puts human beings and their choices at the center.
glossary.religious exemption: Permission to be excused from a rule because following it conflicts with someone's religious beliefs.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.PCB: Printed Circuit Board: a flat board that holds electronic parts and connects them with metal paths.
glossary.PCBA: Printed circuit board assembly: a circuit board with its electronic parts attached.
glossary.Gerber files: Files that show a factory the layers and shapes needed to make a circuit board.
glossary.high-mix: Making many different designs in small batches, rather than lots of copies of one design.
glossary.changeover: The work of adjusting equipment to switch from making one design to another.
glossary.solder paste: A sticky mix of tiny solder particles put on a board before parts are attached.
glossary.reflow: Heating solder until it melts and joins electronic parts to a board.
glossary.quick-turn: A service that makes small batches of boards quickly.
glossary.buried vias: Connections between layers inside a circuit board that do not reach its outer surfaces.
glossary.pick and place: A machine process that picks up electronic parts and puts them in their spots on a board.
glossary.macro: A tool that lets programmers add language features or transform code before it runs.
glossary.Control-R: An add-on that let an editor show changes on a video screen.
glossary.free software movement: A push for software that users can share and improve.
glossary.CNC: Computer Numerical Control: using computer instructions to guide a machine as it cuts or shapes material.
glossary.CAM: Computer aided machining: computer software helps prepare instructions for a machine to carve material.
glossary.toolpaths: Planned routes a machine follows as it carves a piece.
glossary.Gcode: The written instructions that tell a carving machine what to do.
glossary.interpolate: When a machine’s moving parts work together to carve in several directions at once.
glossary.FCC: Federal Communications Commission: the US agency that sets rules for radio equipment.
glossary.spectrum: A range of radio frequencies that wireless devices can use to send signals.
glossary.constellation: A group of satellites that work together to provide a service.
glossary.direct-to-device network: A satellite network designed to connect directly to devices like phones.
glossary.satcom: Satellite communications: sending calls or data through satellites.
glossary.DHS: Department of Homeland Security: the US government department named in the order’s title.
glossary.ICE: Internal Combustion Engine: an engine that makes power by burning fuel inside it.
glossary.CBP: Customs and Border Protection: the US agency whose agents handle border checks.
glossary.Okta: A service organizations use to manage staff sign-ins to work systems.
glossary.permission group: A set of workers allowed to access certain internal systems.
glossary.workpapers: Workpapers are the notes and calculations that show how a tax return or advice was put together.
glossary.derailed: When a train leaves the rails it is meant to run on.
glossary.signalling system: A system that tells train crews when it is safe to move.
glossary.block separation: Keeping trains in separate stretches of track so they do not get too close.
glossary.false positive: A system reports a match even though the person is not the one it was looking for.
glossary.shadow blocked: When a platform quietly limits how widely your posts are shown without clearly telling you.
glossary.phishing: A scam that tricks someone into entering login details on a fake site.
glossary.cURL: A tool for fetching or sending information to a website by typing a command.
glossary.DDoS: Distributed denial-of-service: an attack that floods a service with traffic so people can't use it.
glossary.paywall: A website barrier that asks you to pay before reading an article.
glossary.href: The part of a webpage link that holds the address it leads to.
glossary.malware: Software made to harm a computer or get access to it without permission.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.userspace: The part of a computer where ordinary apps run, rather than the operating system's core.
glossary.package repository: A collection of programs an operating system can install.
glossary.2FA: Two-factor authentication: a sign-in check that asks for a second proof of identity as well as a password.
glossary.PAC: Political action committee: a group that raises money to support candidates or political causes.
glossary.TCPA: Telephone Consumer Protection Act: a US law meant to limit some unwanted calls and texts.
glossary.net worth: What you own minus what you owe.
glossary.percentile: A way to divide a group ranked from lowest to highest into 100 equal-sized slices.
glossary.paper wealth: Value tied up in things like shares, rather than cash you can readily spend.
glossary.wealth tax: A tax based on what someone owns, rather than just what they earn.
glossary.HTTPS: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure: the secure way websites and apps send information over the internet.
glossary.certificate: A digital ID that helps show which website a connection belongs to.
glossary.MITM: Man-in-the-middle: an attack where someone secretly sits between two sides and reads or changes what they send.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the built-in startup software that checks a computer and starts its main software.
glossary.EDK II: An open-source codebase hardware makers and cloud providers use to create UEFI firmware.
glossary.PXE boot: Starting a computer by loading its startup code from a network instead of a drive.
glossary.ICMP: Internet Control Message Protocol: network messages that report errors or help check whether a device can be reached.
glossary.buffer overflow: When a program reads or writes beyond the space set aside for data.
glossary.Secure Boot: A startup check that helps keep untrusted software from loading.
glossary.TPM: Trusted Platform Module: a security component that can hold secret keys used by a device.
glossary.device tree: A file that describes a device’s hardware so Linux knows how to work with it.
glossary.SoC: System on a Chip: a computer’s main processing parts built together on one chip.
glossary.artificial reef: A structure placed underwater to give sea life a place to live and people a place to explore.
glossary.scuttled: Deliberately sunk, usually said of a ship.
glossary.PCBs: Polychlorinated biphenyls: chemicals that can be harmful, so old ships are checked for them.
glossary.sonar: A way to use sound underwater to map the seafloor or find objects.
glossary.Blue Riband: An award for the fastest crossing of the Atlantic by a passenger ship.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.amortized: Spread the cost of something expensive across the years it is used, rather than counting it all at once.
glossary.capital expenditure: Money a company spends on something it expects to use for a long time, rather than an everyday bill.
glossary.S&P 500: A group of 500 large US companies whose share prices are tracked together.
glossary.margins: How much money is left from a sale after paying the costs of making what was sold.
glossary.smallnet: The article's name for services such as Gemini, Finger, Gopher, and Spartan.
glossary.allocator: A part of a program that sets aside and later returns space in the computer for information.
glossary.arena allocator: A memory manager that gives out memory in a group and frees the whole group at once.
glossary.fuzzing: Testing software with lots of varied inputs to see whether it breaks.
glossary.TUI: Terminal User Interface: the menus and controls an app shows inside a text terminal.
glossary.comptime: A Zig feature for doing some work while a program is being built, rather than while it runs.
glossary.incremental compilation: Rebuilding only the parts of a program affected by changes, rather than starting over.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.bootstrap: Getting a compiler built using an earlier tool or a small starter version.
glossary.RAII: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: a way for C++ to clean up things like files automatically when they are no longer needed.
glossary.parameters: Learned values inside a model that shape the answers it gives.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.omni model: A model that works with pictures, sound, and language together.
glossary.hallucination: When an AI gives made-up or incorrect information as if it were true.
glossary.semantic search: A way to find information by what it means, even when it doesn't use the exact words you searched for.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.model: A mathematical setup where the claims or rules in question all hold.
glossary.privilege escalation: A flaw that lets someone get more control of a computer than they should have.
glossary.SSH forwarding: A setting that sends other network traffic through an existing remote login connection.
glossary.ACLs: Access Control Lists: rules that decide which people or devices can reach which computers.
glossary.preclinical: Work on a possible medicine before it is tested in people.
glossary.clinical trial: A study that tests a treatment in people to see whether it works and is safe.
glossary.antibody: A protein the immune system uses to recognize a target; some medicines use these proteins.
glossary.lead: A possible drug that researchers are still trying to improve.
glossary.hit: A design that shows the desired effect in an early test.
glossary.CAR T-cell therapy: A cancer treatment that gives immune cells instructions to recognize cancer cells.
glossary.Lean: A computer program used to write mathematical proofs and check that their steps are correct.
glossary.formalization: Writing mathematics in a precise form that a computer can check.
glossary.finite simple group: A finite mathematical symmetry system that serves as a basic building block for understanding other groups.
glossary.sporadic group: One of 26 exceptional finite simple groups that do not fit the main repeating families.
glossary.auto-formalization: Using software to turn ordinary math proofs into proofs a computer can check.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.cyclomatic complexity: A measure of how many possible routes through a piece of code there are; more routes can make it harder to test.
glossary.just-in-time depth: Learning enough about an unfamiliar problem right when you need to solve it.
glossary.SRE: Site Reliability Engineering: work focused on keeping online services running and fixing them when they break.
glossary.YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It: the idea that you shouldn't build a feature before there's a real need for it.
glossary.debt wall: A large amount of borrowed money comes due around the same time, so borrowers need to repay or replace it.
glossary.private equity: Investment firms that buy whole companies, try to make them earn more, then sell them.
glossary.private credit: Loans from investment firms and other lenders outside the usual bank system.
glossary.write-down wall: A wave of records showing that assets are worth less than they were listed as before.
glossary.BDC: Business Development Companies: organizations that lend money to businesses.
glossary.Forth: A programming language where instructions work with a pile of values, taking from or adding to the top.
glossary.multitasking: Running more than one task in a program, by switching between them or working on them at once.
glossary.message queue: A way for tasks to leave messages for each other and pick them up later, so they can communicate and coordinate.
glossary.actor model: A way to organize a program as separate workers that communicate by sending messages.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.hardware thread: A separate stream of instructions that a processor can run alongside other streams on the same chip.
glossary.Git: A tool for keeping a history of code changes and combining work.
glossary.release point: A published snapshot of the US Code that is current through a particular public law.
glossary.effective-date note: A note saying when a change in a law starts to apply.
glossary.positive law: A title of the US Code Congress has formally enacted as law.
glossary.retroactive: Applied to buildings that already existed, not just ones built later.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
glossary.4F² / 6F²: Names for different shapes and layouts of a DRAM cell; 4F² was expected to offer a theoretical density improvement over 6F².
glossary.3D DRAM: Memory made by stacking multiple layers of DRAM storage cells vertically.
glossary.printhead: The part of an inkjet printer that puts ink onto paper.
glossary.shutter: The camera part that opens briefly to let light in for a picture.
glossary.cherelle wilt: The natural process where young cacao pods dry out instead of continuing to grow.
glossary.cross-pollinate: Move pollen between flowers so they can produce fruit.
glossary.hand-pollinate: Move pollen from one flower to another yourself so the flower can be fertilized.
glossary.midge: A small insect that the article says pollinates cacao flowers.
